episode.lensDescription: What can you DO with this? Practical, tactical, classroom-ready.
episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Wednesday, April 22nd, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers today, college students are increasingly turning to careers they consider more resistant to artificial intelligence automation. According to a Spectrum News 13 investigation, working professionals are returning to college to pursue trades and technical careers as automation fears grow.

At Northbridge University in Kissimmee, Florida, students like Richard Matos are leaving information technology careers for HVAC training, while Mateo Eraso is transitioning from granite installation to electrical work. University President James Michael Burkett said they're seeing two distinct groups: students wanting to upskill or reskill into career fields that are more A.I. resistant, and others learning to integrate A.I. into business and technology roles.

The shift comes as research predicts workforce disruption. Tufts University's Digital Planet research platform identified information, finance, insurance, and professional services as industries with the steepest risks from A.I. over the next two to five years. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics predicts A.I. will impact jobs easily replicated by generative A.I., with medical transcriptionists and customer service representatives expected to see nearly five percent employment decline over seven years.

Construction and extraction occupations, however, are projected to grow rapidly from 2024 to 2034, with more than six hundred forty-nine thousand job openings annually. Burkett emphasized that A.I. is not going to treat the patient in the medical facility or come out and wire houses or work in HVAC when air conditioning breaks down in July.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Case Study today, Penn State made leading A.I. models available to all faculty and staff through A.I. Studio, the university's enterprise generative A.I. platform. According to the university, the platform provides access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google in a single interface. More than one thousand faculty and staff used A.I. Studio during a pilot phase that began in March, with over eighty-five percent of survey respondents saying they would use the platform again. The most common uses were writing and editing, research, and analyzing or summarizing information. A student pilot will run during Summer Session Two, with full rollout to all students at all campuses expected this fall. The platform includes privacy protections: personal information is not used to train A.I. Studio or its underlying models, and conversations will not be provided for academic integrity investigations.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Insights and Trends, Americans want A.I. education but oppose A.I. student services, according to a Quinnipiac University poll. Seventy-four percent of Americans think college students should be taught how to use A.I., but they oppose colleges using A.I. for student services. Americans oppose colleges using A.I. tools to screen student applications by fifty-nine to thirty percent and oppose A.I. tutoring by fifty-two to forty-four percent. The survey revealed sharp age differences: fifty-eight percent of eighteen to thirty-four year olds think college students are more likely to use A.I. to avoid learning rather than help learning, while only thirty-five percent of those sixty-five and older share that concern. The survey of twelve hundred ten adults was conducted April ninth through thirteenth with a margin of error of plus or minus three point five percentage points.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Practical Tips today, a growing number of college instructors are implementing oral exams to address what educators describe as an A.I. crisis in higher education. According to the Associated Press, professors are noticing trends as generative A.I. becomes more sophisticated: take-home essays are coming back perfect, but students can't explain their work when asked. At Cornell University, biomedical engineering professor Chris Schaffer introduced oral defenses where students speak directly to instructors without technology. At the University of Pennsylvania, Emily Hammer pairs oral exams with written papers, noting students are losing skills, losing cognitive capacity and creativity. Several universities now offer faculty workshops on oral exams, representing what Penn's Bruce Lenthall calls a massive shift toward in-person assessments. Student feedback has been mixed but generally positive, with Cornell junior Olivia Piserchia saying the oral defense holds students accountable and helps build technical communication skills needed for careers.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: Penn State Launches AI Studio Platform for Faculty and Staff
leadStory.summary: More than 1,000 faculty and staff tested Penn State's new AI Studio during a pilot phase that began in March, and 85 percent said they would use it again. The university announced this week that AI Studio is now available to all employees beginning April 24, providing access to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini through a single interface at no cost. Pilot participants described using the platform to accelerate research projects, refactor software code, build interactive learning tools, prepare meeting materials, and edit academic papers. The platform supports research, teaching, administrative work, and creative projects across all Penn State campuses. A student pilot will run during Summer Session II, with full rollout to all students at all campuses expected by fall 2026. The phased approach gives faculty time to build familiarity with AI Studio before students gain access. Penn State said personal information is not used to train AI Studio or its underlying AI models, and staff do not monitor individual prompts or conversations. AI Studio joins Microsoft Copilot as part of Penn State's expanding AI tools portfolio, with additional integrations planned for Google Gemini standalone and NotebookLM in future releases. The launch is paired with AI Essentials at Penn State, a foundational AI literacy course designed to equip employees with knowledge and ethical grounding for responsible AI use in daily work. Penn State described AI Studio as enterprise generative AI, meaning it operates within the university's secure infrastructure rather than through public-facing consumer tools. The platform represents one component of Penn State's broader AI strategy announced earlier this academic year.

quickHits.headline: Harvard Requires AI Training Module for All Freshmen
quickHits.summary: Every Harvard College freshman taking expository writing this semester completed a required three-part training module on artificial intelligence, the first time the training has been mandated across the program, The Harvard Crimson reported. More than 90 percent of Harvard College students take an Expos course in their first year to fulfill the writing requirement. The module covers how large language models work, their impact on education, and broader questions about AI and society. Associate Dean of Undergraduate Education Gillian B. Pierce said the module was designed to give every student a shared baseline on generative AI and to relieve faculty of having to teach the basics themselves. The first section walks students through the mechanics of large language models, while the second examines AI effects on education, including published research from Harvard faculty on custom chatbots in physics courses. The third takes up questions of environmental impact, data privacy, copyright, and disinformation. The Harvard College Writing Program developed the training after piloting it in select courses beginning in fall 2024. The module was designed as a starting point rather than a comprehensive treatment, with disciplinary specifics to be addressed in later coursework.

quickHits.headline: Americans Want AI Education But Doubt Student Learning Benefits
quickHits.summary: Seventy-four percent of Americans think it is important that college students be taught how to use AI, but 47 percent believe students are more likely to use AI to avoid learning rather than help them learn, a new Quinnipiac University poll found. The survey reveals a sharp generational divide in perceptions of AI use in education. Among 18 to 34 year olds, 58 percent think students use AI to avoid learning, compared to just 35 percent of those 65 and older. Americans also oppose colleges using AI tools in screening student applications by a 59 to 30 percent margin and oppose AI tutoring by 52 to 44 percent. The poll of 1,210 adults nationwide was conducted April 9-13 with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Despite skepticism about AI applications, 78 percent of Americans with an associate's degree or higher say their college degree was worth it, citing job opportunities, salaries and quality education as major reasons. Seventy-six percent of Americans think international students studying in the U.S. is good for the country, with different perspectives benefiting American students cited as the top reason.

quickHits.headline: University of Cincinnati Launches BearcatGPT for Students and Faculty
quickHits.summary: University of Cincinnati students have created dozens of AI-powered study guides, tutoring tools, and digital assistants since BearcatGPT opened to them in February, WLWT reported. The platform provides UC students, faculty, and staff with access to AI tools that do not require sharing data in the public domain. Agents being used by students include Bearcat Study Pal, Bearcat Test-Prepper, and Bearcat Genius. Bharath Prabhakaran, UC vice president and chief digital officer, said the platform gives the UC community access to a suite of private AI tools while ensuring data remains private and secure. UC unveiled BearcatGPT to faculty last year before opening it to students this spring. The platform is part of UC's Bearcats AI Ready initiative, which Prabhakaran described as an element of the university's Next Lives Here strategic direction focused on innovation and digital transformation. UC is the first university in Ohio to offer such a platform and among the first in the country to provide a private, secure AI environment for its campus community.

quickHits.headline: Cornell Professor Replaces Written Homework Grades with Oral Defenses
quickHits.summary: Cornell biomedical engineering professor Chris Schaffer stopped grading written homework assignments last semester. His students now complete problem sets but only their oral defenses count toward their grades, Fortune reported. The 20-minute sessions use Socratic-style questioning, with Schaffer and teaching assistants sharing evaluation duties for his 70-student class. Schaffer made the change after noticing students submitted perfect take-home essays but could not explain their work when questioned. He told Fortune that oral exams reveal whether students actually understand the material. Cornell junior Olivia Piserchia said she initially found the oral defense nerve-wracking but came to value the one-on-one interaction. She noted the accountability factor differs from written work. "It is a lot harder to look people in the eyes and say out loud that you do not know something," she said. Cornell's Center for Teaching Innovation now highlights Schaffer's approach in its Oral Assessment Workshop, which has drawn interest from faculty across departments looking for alternatives to traditional written assessments.
